citation: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622
title: EyeRIS gaze-contingent display control system with Dual Purkinje Image eyetracking for retinal stabilization
description: EyeRIS is "a custom-developed system based on dedicated hardware, which allows flexible gaze-contingent display control." It acquires eye movement signals from a Dual Purkinje Image eyetracker (spatial resolution 1′, sampled at 1 kHz), processes them in real time, and updates the display to compensate for eye movements, keeping stimuli at fixed foveal eccentricities. Combined with a two-step gaze-contingent calibration procedure, it enabled the first tests of selective attention within the foveola, with a stabilization error of approximately 1′ and a 10 ms system delay.
requirements: High spatial and temporal resolution eye tracking and a two-step gaze-contingent calibration procedure to map eyetracker output into visual angles
constraints: Trials with delay exceeding 14 ms were discarded, and analyses were restricted to trials with good stabilization quality (blinks, saccades, and late microsaccades excluded)
target_learning_goals: precise control of retinal stimulation for studying spatial attention
examples: Stimuli were moved in real time under EyeRIS control to compensate for observer eye movements during Experiments 2 and 3
key_sources: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622

article_title: Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm
citation: Nückles, M. (2021). Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09567-5
title: An emerging research paradigm joining four originally separated research strands on visual perception in teaching and learning
description: The article characterizes an emerging research paradigm in which eye-tracking methodologies are used to study professional vision and teacher expertise. It argues the paradigm brings together "different and originally separated strands of research": professional vision in teacher education, expertise structure and development in cognitive science, eye-tracking study of cognitive processes in psychology, and educational effectiveness and instructional quality research. The seven special-issue contributions instantiate this paradigm.
requirements: Advanced eye-tracking technologies, including mobile eye-tracking glasses, to study gaze in naturalistic classroom settings
constraints: The paradigm is at an early stage; the author identifies theoretical assumptions in it that he considers controversial
target_learners: teachers and teacher students in professional development
target_learning_goals: professional vision
teacher expertise
instructional quality
examples: The seven contributions of the special issue each combine at least two of the four strands, e.g., expert-novice comparisons using mobile eye-tracking during real lessons
key_sources: Nückles, M. (2021). Investigating Visual Perception in Teaching and Learning with Advanced Eye-Tracking Methodologies: Rewards and Challenges of an Innovative Research Paradigm. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09567-5

article_title: Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning
citation: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9
title: Four-component validity scoring scheme for eye-tracking measures (0–4 points)
description: A structured scoring system adapted from Cook et al. and Naismith and Cavalcanti for evaluating validity evidence of eye-tracking measures, comprising four components: content, relations with other variables, data quality, and consequences. "The total validity score was calculated by summing the scores across all four components, yielding possible scores ranging from 0 to 4." Internal structure and response process were reinterpreted as data quality for eye tracking. The scheme enabled comparison of validity strength across learning constructs in the review.
requirements: Validity evidence from accumulated studies must be available for each component to assign points
constraints: Originally designed for broader measurement tools such as questionnaires and observation, requiring adaptation for eye-tracking methodologies
target_learners: Researchers evaluating eye-tracking measures in IVR learning environments
target_learning_goals: Evaluating and improving measurement validity of learning-process indicators
examples: Applied to score eye-tracking measures across 38 studies, with component scores reported per construct
key_sources: Lee, J. Y., Moon, J., Paas, F., Cho, M., Darejeh, A., Holmer, S., & Ayres, P. (2026). Validity of Eye-Tracking Measures in Immersive Virtual Reality: Using Cognitive Theories of Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10186-9

article_title: What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue
citation: Kaakinen, J. K. (2021). What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue. Educational Psychology Review, 33, 169-179. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09573-7
title: Eye movement data analysis should use measures and statistical methods that capture the time-course of processing and the data's correlational structure
description: The author argues that eye tracking's main advantage is detailed time-course information, which total fixation time or gaze duration fails to exploit because it "sums up all fixations or gazes made to a particular area of interest." She recommends first-pass and reinspection measures, fixation probability over time, and scanpath analysis, and notes that traditional ANOVA or t test approaches are often not optimal because eye movement data have correlational structure, missing observations, and unbalanced data.
requirements: AOI definitions should be guided by theory and support hypothesis testing; statistical methods must handle correlational structure, missing observations, and unbalanced data.
constraints: Mixed-effects methods require sufficient statistical power, which depends on the number of participants and observations per participant; recruiting classroom participants is difficult.
target_learning_goals: valid analysis of visual perception and attention processes in learning contexts
examples: The author notes linear mixed models are the gold standard in reading research, with Poisson models for fixation counts and mixed logit models for fixation probability.
key_sources: Kaakinen, J. K. (2021). What Can Eye Movements Tell us about Visual Perception Processes in Classroom Contexts? Commentary on a Special Issue. Educational Psychology Review, 33, 169-179. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09573-7

article_title: Taking a closer look at how higher education students process and use (discrepant) peer feedback
citation: Van Meenen, F., Masson, N., Catrysse, L., & Coertjens, L. (2023). Taking a closer look at how higher education students process and use (discrepant) peer feedback. Learning and Instruction, 84, 101711. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101711
title: Eye-tracking paradigm for studying peer feedback processing and use
description: A laboratory paradigm in which 59 higher education students read the feedback of two peers on a fictional essay and revise it while their gaze behaviour is recorded. It separates a PF processing subphase (transitions, first-pass reading times) from a PF use subphase (dwell time on essay, revision quality assessed by professors), enabling process-level measurement of feedback uptake.
requirements: Eye-tracking equipment and professor-assessed revision quality ratings
constraints: Studied with a fictional essay task in higher education
target_learning_goals: understanding and improving peer feedback uptake
examples: We asked 59 participants to read the feedback of two peers on a fictional essay and to revise it, while we recorded their gaze behaviour
key_sources: Van Meenen, F., Masson, N., Catrysse, L., & Coertjens, L. (2023). Taking a closer look at how higher education students process and use (discrepant) peer feedback. Learning and Instruction, 84, 101711. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101711

article_title: The Role of Eye Movement Consistency in Aging-Related Decline in Face Recognition
citation: Zheng, Y., Lo, T. W., Lau, E. Y., Eskes, G., Hui, L. L., & Hsiao, J. H. (2026). The Role of Eye Movement Consistency in Aging-Related Decline in Face Recognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00437-3
title: Eye movement consistency as an index of visual routine quality: the inverted-U lifespan account
description: The article frames face recognition as depending on visual routines — consistent, learned scanning patterns — whose quality is indexed by eye movement entropy measured with EMHMM. During development, children show decreasing entropy as routines form; adults show stable low-entropy idiosyncratic routines; and in middle-to-older adulthood entropy rises again, suggesting "an inverted U shape across the lifespan". The account holds that aging-related decline in consistency reflects difficulty executing, not forgetting, learned routines, tied to declining selective attention and inhibitory control and possibly fixation noise from sensorimotor decline.
requirements: Eye tracking during face recognition and EMHMM modeling to quantify pattern (E-N scale) and consistency (overall and C3 entropy)
Interpretation of entropy as routine quality presumes a learned visual routine from extensive face recognition experience in early adulthood
constraints: The article reports the age distribution concentrated between 50 and 70, which may affect aging-related correlations and limit generalizability outside this range
The sample was restricted to Asian participants processing Asian faces, so generalization to other cultural groups remains unclear
Younger adult faces only were used, leaving own-age bias unexamined
The study used a cross-sectional design; longitudinal work is needed to trace lifespan changes
target_learners: middle-aged and older adults (40–81 years old)
target_learning_goals: face recognition and the visual scanning and attentional strategies that support it
examples: The article suggests future work examine whether training older adults to restore earlier visual routines by enhancing eye movement consistency could mitigate face recognition decline
key_sources: Zheng, Y., Lo, T. W., Lau, E. Y., Eskes, G., Hui, L. L., & Hsiao, J. H. (2026). The Role of Eye Movement Consistency in Aging-Related Decline in Face Recognition. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00437-3

article_title: Virtual reality simulation and real-life training programs for cataract surgery: a scoping review of the literature.
citation: Dormegny Lea, Lansingh Van Charles, Lejay Anne, Chakfe Nabil, Yaici Rémi, Sauer Arnaud, Gaucher David, Henderson Bonnie An, Thomsen Ann Sofia Skou, Bourcier Tristan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation and real-life training programs for cataract surgery: a scoping review of the literature. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06245-w
title: EyeSi and HelpMeSee virtual reality cataract surgery simulators
description: Two widely used virtual reality simulators for cataract surgery training. EyeSi is "a widespread, commercially-available cataract surgery simulator designed for phacoemulsification and vitreoretinal surgery self-guided training" mostly used in high-income countries. HelpMeSee "focuses on resource-limited areas in low- and middle-income countries", mainly training manual small incision cataract surgery with certified instructors and a reimbursement system. The review compared outcomes across 13 EyeSi studies and one HMS study.
requirements: Access to the simulator hardware, which the review notes is limited by acquisition and maintenance cost
constraints: EyeSi is mostly located in high-income countries while HMS is primarily found in low- and middle-income countries, illustrating unequal access to the technology
target_learners: Allied health personnel in resource-limited areas (HMS)
target_learning_goals: Cataract surgical skills (phacoemulsification, MSICS)
Patient safety in the operating room
examples: The HMS study in India used a 6-day, 35-hour training with 80% HMS simulator time plus a supervised surgery phase on actual patients
key_sources: Dormegny Lea, Lansingh Van Charles, Lejay Anne, Chakfe Nabil, Yaici Rémi, Sauer Arnaud, Gaucher David, Henderson Bonnie An, Thomsen Ann Sofia Skou, Bourcier Tristan. (2024). Virtual reality simulation and real-life training programs for cataract surgery: a scoping review of the literature. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06245-w

article_title: Simulation training in vitreoretinal surgery: a systematic review.
citation: Rasmussen Rasmus Christian, Grauslund Jakob, Vergmann Anna Stage. (2019). Simulation training in vitreoretinal surgery: a systematic review. BMC Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12886-019-1098-x
title: EyeSi Surgical Simulator for vitreoretinal training and assessment
description: The EyeSi Surgical Simulator (VRMagic, Mannheim, Germany) is a virtual reality simulator for ophthalmic microsurgical training. Five of the seven studies included in the review "all used the same virtual reality simulator, the EyeSi® Surgical Simulator," training skills subcategorized as complex procedures, intraocular navigation and instrument handling. The review concludes it can be used to assess and possibly improve basic and complex VRS skills, with expert groups showing no performance improvement across sessions.
requirements: Instrument validation reporting, which the review found lacking in most studies using it
constraints: No evidence currently supports transfer of training on it to the operating room
target_learners: medical students, ophthalmic residents and fellows training in vitreoretinal surgery
target_learning_goals: intraocular navigation, instrument handling, and complex procedures such as membrane peeling and vitrectomy
examples: Studies in the review used it for navigation tasks with orbs varying in size and distance to retina, epiretinal membrane peeling, and multi-module overall scoring across repeated sessions
key_sources: Rasmussen Rasmus Christian, Grauslund Jakob, Vergmann Anna Stage. (2019). Simulation training in vitreoretinal surgery: a systematic review. BMC Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12886-019-1098-x

article_title: A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology.
citation: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1
title: Eyesi Surgical virtual reality ophthalmic surgery simulator
description: The Eyesi Surgical (VRmagic, Mannheim, Germany) is "a high-fidelity virtual reality simulator designed for practising intraocular procedures". It combines a mannequin head housing a model eye, an operating microscope, instrument tracking sensors, and software modules for cataract and vitreoretinal surgery steps; the system records performance metrics, enabling scores and feedback to be generated. It is the most extensively assessed ophthalmic simulator in the review, with 33 validity studies.
requirements: Requires the hardware suite (mannequin head, model eye, operative microscope, instruments, foot pedals, touchscreen) and the VR software platform with its training modules.
constraints: Comprehensive validity evidence exists for the cataract modules; response-processes evidence remained limited even there.
target_learning_goals: cataract surgery skills
vitreoretinal surgery skills
examples: Studies in the review trained participants on forceps, anti-tremor, capsulorhexis and phacoemulsification tasks, with training times ranging from 20 minutes to mastery-learning formats.
key_sources: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1

article_title: Teaching ophthalmic microsurgical skills: conventional microscopy versus heads-up visualization.
citation: Eckardt F, Gerhardt M, Priglinger S. (2026). Teaching ophthalmic microsurgical skills: conventional microscopy versus heads-up visualization. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10269-9
title: EyeSi Surgical Simulator with 3D heads-up visualization system for microsurgical training
description: The EyeSi® Surgical Simulator (Haag-Streit, Köniz, Switzerland) is a virtual reality simulator providing validated training modules for cataract and vitreoretinal surgery with objective performance metrics and the possibility of repeated practice. In this study it was equipped with both a conventional ocular microscope and a 3D heads-up display, and automatically generated objective performance metrics including overall performance scores, precision parameters, error rates, and task completion times.
requirements: A 3D heads-up visualization system and conventional microscopic visualization with oculars available on the simulator platform.
constraints: The article notes simulator performance cannot be assumed to directly reflect operative performance or clinical competency.
target_learning_goals: Cataract and vitreoretinal surgical skills including anti-tremor control, bimanual coordination, and spatial navigation
examples: Participants completed three training exercises in a cataract surgery setting and three in a vitreoretinal surgery setting, after a standardized 10-minute familiarization phase.
key_sources: Eckardt F, Gerhardt M, Priglinger S. (2026). Teaching ophthalmic microsurgical skills: conventional microscopy versus heads-up visualization. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10269-9

article_title: A MOOC-based and high-fidelity surgical simulation-integrated clinical internship mode in optometry teaching for ophthalmology graduate students.
citation: Yang K, Kanwen W, Jing C, Zidan G, Chenggong J, Xue L. (2026). A MOOC-based and high-fidelity surgical simulation-integrated clinical internship mode in optometry teaching for ophthalmology graduate students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09610-z
title: Eyesi Ophthalmology high-fidelity virtual reality surgical simulator for refractive surgery training
description: The HFS system was a high-fidelity ophthalmic surgical simulator (Eyesi Ophthalmology, VRmagic GmbH, Germany) integrating "virtual reality display, a microscopic surgical interface, and a force-feedback tactile system." For refractive surgery training it "simulates the complete procedure of femtosecond laser-assisted laser in situ keratomileusis (FS-LASIK) from a first-person surgeon's view." Its built-in software "automatically generated objective performance reports for each procedure" and provided guidance. The authors note it does not involve patient-specific digital twin technology based on image fitting or clinical data fusion.
requirements: Progressive tasks with repeated practice at key stages until proficiency
Standardized simulator-based assessments before and after training to quantify skill improvement
constraints: Does not involve patient-specific digital twin technology based on image fitting or clinical data fusion
target_learners: Ophthalmology graduate students training in refractive surgery
target_learning_goals: FS-LASIK procedural skills
Objective assessment of surgical skill improvement
examples: Students practiced repeatedly using the simulator until proficiency was achieved during the Day 6 classroom session of the blended internship.
key_sources: Yang K, Kanwen W, Jing C, Zidan G, Chenggong J, Xue L. (2026). A MOOC-based and high-fidelity surgical simulation-integrated clinical internship mode in optometry teaching for ophthalmology graduate students. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09610-z

article_title: Application of Mixed Reality for Ophthalmic Clinical Skills and Diagnosis: Prospective Study.
citation: Tan CJM, Yong WWD, Lin HHA, Oh J, Yong HSR, Khew FMJ, Shen L, Gao Y, Kow WCA, Tham YC, Liu D, Cheng CY, Ngiam KY, Yuen YS, Manotosh R, Khoo ET, Koh TCV, Tan WTC. (2026). Application of Mixed Reality for Ophthalmic Clinical Skills and Diagnosis: Prospective Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71338
title: EyelearnMR mixed reality simulation application for ocular motility examination on HoloLens 2
description: EyelearnMR is a mixed reality simulation application "designed to teach and assess ocular examination via a wearable headset," consisting of a hologram 3D patient, a Lang fixation cube for ocular motility examination, and animation logic modeling eye movements during fixation. Deployed on Microsoft HoloLens 2, it superimposes simulated patients in physical space and offers six simulated ocular motility scenarios that students practice in guided 2-hour sessions, enabling repeated, standardized practice with reproducible clinical signs.
requirements: A HoloLens 2 headset; the study used six HoloLens units for the deployment
constraints: The HoloLens 2 has a limited field of view (43° horizontally versus the human 135°) and roughly 2 hours of battery life; student feedback highlighted tracking-accuracy issues; results cover only ocular motility and cannot be extrapolated to other clinical skills
target_learners: fourth-year undergraduate medical students on an ophthalmology rotation
target_learning_goals: ocular motility examination technique
recognition of clinical signs
diagnostic reasoning
examples: Students in the intervention arm completed an additional 2-hour guided practice session with EyelearnMR on days 8 and 9 of their posting; control students experienced the modules for 2 hours at the end of the posting

article_title: Situation Awareness Assessment for Anesthesia Residents (SAAAR): Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Multimodal System.
citation: Carolina Daza-Beltrán, Angélica Paola Fajardo Escolar, Martha Caro, Daniel R. Suárez (2026). Situation Awareness Assessment for Anesthesia Residents (SAAAR): Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Multimodal System. Human Factors. https://doi.org/10.1177/00187208251413484
title: Use eye-tracking data as a prompt for guided reflection rather than as a standalone evaluative metric in formative situation awareness assessment
description: In formative assessment, gaze data should not be scored in isolation: the SAAAR reviews gaze-overlay videos during debriefing, where "eye-tracking data functioned as a prompt for guided reflection rather than as a standalone evaluative metric". Ambiguous behaviors such as brief glances are examined with residents, who explain their intentions and reasoning, mitigating subjective interpretation and accessing situation awareness as a cognitive process.
requirements: Gaze-overlay recordings from the scenario and a structured video debriefing session in which residents can explain their intentions, reasoning, and contextual constraints.
constraints: The article states quantitative eye-tracking processing "requires specialized software and delays analysis, limiting its applicability for real-time reflection".
target_learning_goals: situation awareness as a cognitive process
guided reflection and targeted feedback
examples: In a blood transfusion simulation, gaze-overlay review showing that residents had not checked the blood unit information was discussed during debriefing, where residents explained their reasoning and received targeted feedback.
key_sources: Carolina Daza-Beltrán, Angélica Paola Fajardo Escolar, Martha Caro, Daniel R. Suárez (2026). Situation Awareness Assessment for Anesthesia Residents (SAAAR): Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Multimodal System. Human Factors. https://doi.org/10.1177/00187208251413484

article_title: Ophthalmic surgical simulator: an effective and safe approach for trainees in vitreoretinal surgery.
citation: Giannuzzi Federico, Hu Lorenzo, Carlà Matteo Mario, Cestrone Valentina, Marcelli Sofia, De Vico Umberto, Savastano Alfonso, Crincoli Emanuele, Savastano Maria Cristina, Rizzo Stanislao. (2025). Ophthalmic surgical simulator: an effective and safe approach for trainees in vitreoretinal surgery. International Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10792-025-03851-5
title: EyeSi Surgical Simulator vitreoretinal training module
description: The EyeSi Surgical Simulator (VRmagic, Mannheim, Germany) is a virtual reality platform for ophthalmic surgical training, offering "an immersive and risk-free environment where trainees can safely develop and refine their surgical skills". Its vitreoretinal module replicates posterior segment surgery tasks such as membrane peeling, retinal detachment repair, and laser photocoagulation, using tactile feedback, a stereoscopic display, a BIOM-like optical system, and foot pedal controls. Trainees in this study completed Module-B, Level 2 on Navigation and Instruments Laser Coagulation, and the simulator reports a performance score (maximum 100) based on five criteria: target achievement, efficiency, instrument handling, microscope handling, and tissue treatment.
requirements: Trainees require basic cataract surgery proficiency; a minimum of 20 cataract procedures performed as primary surgeon was required for inclusion in this study
constraints: The substantial cost of the EyeSi simulator remains a key limitation, potentially limiting its accessibility in smaller or resource-limited training programs
target_learning_goals: vitreoretinal surgical skills including depth perception, fine motor control, and spatial awareness
examples: Trainees completed Module-B, Level 2 on Navigation and Instruments Laser Coagulation, requiring identification of four peripheral retinal holes and surrounding each with at least two contiguous rows of laser spots
key_sources: Giannuzzi Federico, Hu Lorenzo, Carlà Matteo Mario, Cestrone Valentina, Marcelli Sofia, De Vico Umberto, Savastano Alfonso, Crincoli Emanuele, Savastano Maria Cristina, Rizzo Stanislao. (2025). Ophthalmic surgical simulator: an effective and safe approach for trainees in vitreoretinal surgery. International Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10792-025-03851-5

article_title: EYE-ECG2: Addressing medical student feedback in an RCT with eye-tracking videos featuring cued retrospective reporting and modified learning sequences for ECG interpretation skills training.
citation: Scherff Aline D., Kääb Stefan, Fischer Martin R., Berndt Markus. (2025). EYE-ECG2: Addressing medical student feedback in an RCT with eye-tracking videos featuring cued retrospective reporting and modified learning sequences for ECG interpretation skills training. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume42/zma001771
title: EYE-ECG2 video: expert eye-tracking gaze cues synchronised with cued retrospective reporting commentary
description: The EYE-ECG2 video is a learning intervention in which a senior cardiology expert's eye movements, recorded with a head-mounted eye-tracker while interpreting 15 authentic patient ECGs, are projected onto the ECG images "visualised as a moving red focus spot with a trail marking previously viewed locations", combined with the expert's cued retrospective reporting audio commentary. Its modification over the predecessor video holds the gaze marker stationary while the corresponding verbal explanation plays, synchronising visual focus with verbal explication. It was given to the intervention group in addition to standard ECG training.
requirements: Students must watch the entire video at least once without interruption; participants could freely pause, rewind, or re-watch it at their discretion
constraints: The synchronisation was performed on pre-existing materials with no new recordings; all visual and auditory material was preserved unchanged in order and content
target_learners: medical students who have completed their university cardiology module
target_learning_goals: ECG interpretation skills
clinical reasoning and diagnostic visual search
examples: In the RCT, the intervention group (n=47) watched the 12m 04s video for M=14.36min (SD=3.06) within the online training session
key_sources: Scherff Aline D., Kääb Stefan, Fischer Martin R., Berndt Markus. (2025). EYE-ECG2: Addressing medical student feedback in an RCT with eye-tracking videos featuring cued retrospective reporting and modified learning sequences for ECG interpretation skills training. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume42/zma001771

article_title: EYE-ECG: An RCT of the influence of student characteristics and expert eye-tracking videos with cued retrospective reporting on students' ECG interpretation skills.
citation: Scherff Aline D., Kääb Stefan, Fischer Martin R., Berndt Markus. (2024). EYE-ECG: An RCT of the influence of student characteristics and expert eye-tracking videos with cued retrospective reporting on students’ ECG interpretation skills. GMS Journal for Medical Education 41(4):Doc40. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2024-41/zma001695.shtml
title: EYE-ECG video: expert eye-tracking gaze video with cued retrospective reporting audio commentary
description: A newly developed instructional video presenting a cardiology expert's real-time gaze pattern during ECG interpretation together with the expert's spoken thought processes. As the article describes it, "Combining all 15 video clips – obtained via eye-tracked expert ECG interpretation – with their CRR audio commentary resulted in a single (EYE-ECG) video of 9m 13s". It was shown to the intervention group after a pre-test as the only difference from the training-as-usual condition, and participants were instructed to watch it fully at least once.
requirements: Learners must watch the full video at least once; it is added on top of standard case-based training
constraints: In the trial it was tested as a single 9-minute addition within a longer online session for advanced (4th/5th-year) medical students
target_learners: advanced medical students in study years four to five
target_learning_goals: ECG interpretation skills
examples: Intervention group students watched the video within a 5-hour maximum online session that also included questionnaires, pre-test, four clinical cases, and post-test

article_title: Eyesi direct ophthalmoscope simulator: an effective training tool for medical undergraduates.
citation: Liu Canying, Lin Jicheng, Wu Siting, Zhu Yingting, Zou Yuxian, Zhang Qi, Li Zhidong, Zhuo Yehong, Li Yiqing. (2024). Eyesi direct ophthalmoscope simulator: an effective training tool for medical undergraduates. BMC Medical Education 24:783. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05780-w
title: Eyesi Direct Ophthalmoscope Simulator
description: The Eyesi Direct Ophthalmoscope Simulator (Model EDO491, VRmagic GMBH, Mannheim, Germany) "simulates the shape and all functions of a real direct ophthalmoscope and reaction of patients such as the changing of pupil size with the lighting level." It provides a built-in case database for independent learning, a test mode for evaluating skill mastery, timely feedback on retinal disease in the inspected area, and teacher guidance via a monitoring screen with real-time operation scores through the VRmNet service. Training progresses from handle construction through landmark identification under mydriatic and normal pupils to diagnosing lesions from typical cases.
requirements: Requires instructor monitoring through the connected screen and the VRmNet service for real-time scoring and guidance
constraints: The simulator is limited to typical retinal lesions, contrasting with diverse and rare conditions in actual clinical practice; the authors emphasize it serves as a complement to, rather than a replacement for, real patient experiences
target_learners: general practitioners in primary medical institutions
target_learning_goals: direct ophthalmoscopy fundus examination skill
recognition of retinal structures and common retinal diseases
examples: Participants learned landmark identification under mydriatic and normal pupillary conditions, assessed cup-to-disc ratio, and monitored examined (bright zone) versus unexamined (dark zone) areas on the monitor

article_title: Implementation of microsurgery simulation in an ophthalmology clerkship in Germany: a prospective, exploratory study.
citation: Deuchler Svenja, Scholtz Julia, Ackermann Hanns, Seitz Berthold, Koch Frank. (2022). Implementation of microsurgery simulation in an ophthalmology clerkship in Germany: a prospective, exploratory study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03634-x
title: Eyesi Surgical virtual reality microsurgery simulator with graded Navigation Training curriculum
description: The Eyesi Surgical simulator from Haag-Streit Simulation is a virtual reality tool that "enables trainees to practice microscopic intraocular surgery in a realistic simulated environment." It uses "a binocular operating microscope, surgical instruments, a patient with mechanical eye, and foot pedals" and its curriculum "begins with basic skills practice and progressively advances users through anterior or posterior segment surgical tasks." In this study students completed Navigation Training Level 1, an abstract targeting task with 19 spheres, scored 0–100 across five criteria categories.
requirements: Supervisor-led introductory lecture and demonstration before practical training
Simulator software (version 3.4) with scored modules providing objective numeric feedback
constraints: Training in the study was limited to up to two sessions during the clerkship
The study used only the abstract Navigation Training Level 1 module, not the clinical surgical modules
target_learners: 10th-semester German medical students during their ophthalmology clerkship
ophthalmology residents and surgeons learning cataract and vitreoretinal surgery
target_learning_goals: basic microsurgical targeting and instrument-navigation skills under the microscope
confidence with microsurgical techniques before live intraocular surgery
examples: Students began with Navigation Training Level 1 and progressed through a maximum of 5 additional modules over two sessions, reviewing a performance summary after each level
